new_statements.quote: If a word does not contain a partial reduplication then stress is assigned within the boundaries of the following morpheme classes. a) Verbs b) Nominal Stems c) Polysyllabic suffixes (monosyllabic suffixes count as part of the stem) d) Adverbs prefixed to, and part nominals compounded in verbs e) Polysyllabic pronominal prefixes, and polysyllabic sequences of pronominal prefixes. Primary stress is assigned to the first syllable with secondary stresses being placed on every second syllable thereafter, subject to the proviso that no syllable receives secondary stress if it is word final or if it precedes a syllable with primary stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not assigned to the phonological word as a whole but to morphological domains inside it: each verb root, nominal stem, polysyllabic suffix, incorporated adverb/nominal, and polysyllabic pronominal prefix (sequence) is a stress domain, and primary stress falls on the FIRST syllable of each such domain, with secondary stresses on alternate syllables after it. Monosyllabic suffixes are part of the stem; monosyllabic pronominal prefixes normally never take stress, so the word-initial syllable is often unstressed (e.g. kat-tjápul-m-al 'I was not smoking'). A word can therefore carry several primary stresses; Harvey says the chief function of stress is to mark internal (compound, reduplication, morpheme) boundaries within the word. Compounds and complete reduplications are treated as two words for stress. Also on p. 36: 'The placement of stress is a complex phenomenon. It is determined by 1. Partial reduplication boundaries 2. Morpheme boundaries.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses fall on every second syllable after the primary within the domain, but never on a word-final syllable and never on a syllable immediately preceding a primary-stressed syllable; in partially reduplicated words secondary stresses go on every second syllable on either side of the primaries (p. 37-38).
new_statements.exceptions: Partial reduplication overrides the morpheme-boundary rule: each part of a partial reduplication gets primary stress on its initial syllable (púkpúkpanj 'fish sp.', mak:ínjik:ínji 'wild passionfruit', tátmepáwukpáwuk 'plant sp.', an-pítpít:-u 'red'); this can put stress on a normally unstressed monosyllabic prefix two syllables away (át-mekkílkíl-m-inj 'I burped'); an open-monosyllable partial reduplication gets stress only if it marks a morphological category (kat-tjá-tjápul-m-al 'I never used to smoke') and not when inherent in the word (kúkutúngunj 'duck sp.', not kúkútungunj). Verbal reduplication is described as messy and possibly affected by language death.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: a word is delimited by pauses (§2.3.1), but stress domains are morphological units inside the word, with multiple primaries per word; compounds and complete reduplications behave as separate words for stress (§2.3.2). Based on elicitation with one fluent speaker, Mrs Doris White (Litawi), of a then-dying language.
new_statements.identity_note: Harvey 1986 calls the language 'Waray' and locates it in the Margaret and upper Adelaide River valleys south-east of Darwin; this is Warray wara1290 (ISO wrz), not the Philippine Waray-Waray (war). The description rests on elicitation from a single fluent speaker (Mrs Doris White, Litawi); no dialect division is described.
